RagShortTexts: The azure shield with golden fleurs-de-lis and the sacred Oriflamme embodied Capetian.

Variants.Content: Under Louis IX the azure shield semy of golden fleurs-de-lis, known as France Ancien, stood as the premier royal arms. The three petals were read as a sign of the Holy Trinity, and the blue field echoed the Virgin, whose devotion the French crown promoted with special fervour. Beside the lilies flew the Oriflamme, the red silk banner kept at the abbey of Saint-Denis and carried into battle only when the king had resolved to fight to the end. Unfurling it meant no quarter would be asked or given. The arms appeared on coins, seals, charters, and the gates of royal fortresses, so every subject who read a document or paid a toll saw the same mark of royal authority.

The lilies of France commanded deference from barons across Christendom. A vassal who held his fief from the Crown measured his standing by how near his own arms sat to the royal shield. A baron who quarrelled with the king could expect his dues to be questioned, so the lily carried an unspoken threat along with its honour.

The iris embodies both Marian purity and regal wisdom. Anointed with holy chrism at Reims under the sign of the lilies, Capetian kings are believed by pilgrims to cure scrofula through the royal touch.
